Q1817102.t: Wild peaks where the Nahanni carves its canyons
Q1817102.s: Almost roadless and nearly empty of people, the Mackenzie Mountains stretch along the border of Yukon and the Northwest Territories. From cruise height you see bare grey ridges, braided rivers and, in autumn, tundra turning red and gold. At their southern end the South Nahanni River carves deep canyons and plunges over Virginia Falls, about twice the height of Niagara.
Q1817102.w: Bare, grey, folded ridges and wide braided rivers, with almost no roads or settlements in sight.
f: In 1978 Nahanni National Park became one of the first places listed as UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
Keele Peak, about 2,950 m, is the highest point of the range.

q.q: Which famous falls lie on the South Nahanni River?

Q1132302.t: Bolivia’s Royal Range, a snowy wall above the Altiplano
Q1132302.s: East of the Altiplano rises a line of high, often snowy peaks — the Cordillera Real, the “Royal Range”. At its northern end Illimani, 6,438 m, towers over La Paz, its white bulk visible from much of the city. Further south the mountains grow drier and redder, cradling Potosí, which grew rich on the silver of Cerro Rico.
Q1132302.w: A wall of snowy peaks and glaciers east of the flat, brown Altiplano, with deep valleys dropping away on the far side.
f: Potosí, at about 4,000 m, was one of the richest cities in the world in the 16th and 17th centuries, thanks to its silver.
The range’s glaciers help supply water to La Paz and El Alto.

q.q: Which mountain towers over La Paz?

ne-rg-1159103969.t: Peru’s western wall of volcanoes and deep canyons
ne-rg-1159103969.s: Between the coastal desert and the high puna, Peru’s Western Cordillera rises as a chain of snow-capped volcanoes — Coropuna, Ampato, Misti. Rivers have sawn canyons through it, and Colca and Cotahuasi are among the deepest on Earth, over 3 km from rim to river. From 11 km up, look for white cones standing on brown plateaus, with the desert falling away towards the Pacific.
ne-rg-1159103969.w: Snow-capped volcanic cones on a high brown plateau, deep dark canyons, and bare desert slopes falling towards the ocean.
f: Coropuna, about 6,400 m, is the highest volcano in Peru.
The Colca Canyon is famous for Andean condors riding the morning updrafts.
The Nazca Lines lie on the desert plain at the western foot of this cordillera.

q.q: Which is the highest volcano in Peru?

ne-rg-1159103969-2.t: The Andes’ westernmost ridge, facing the rainy Chocó
ne-rg-1159103969-2.s: In Colombia the Andes split into three parallel ranges, and this is the westernmost. On its Pacific side lies the Chocó, one of the rainiest regions on Earth, draped in rainforest and usually under cloud; to the east the Cauca River runs through a deep valley. Southwards the same range continues into Ecuador, where it carries the ice-capped Chimborazo.
ne-rg-1159103969-2.w: A forested ridge with cloud piled up on its western, Pacific side and the deep Cauca valley on its eastern side.
f: Towns in the Chocó below its western slopes are among the rainiest places on Earth.
Because Earth bulges at the equator, Chimborazo’s summit is the point on its surface farthest from the planet’s centre.
The steep Farallones de Cali, part of the range, rise just west of the city of Cali.

q.q: Which summit of this range is farthest from Earth’s centre?

Q804330.t: The White Range: the tropics’ greatest mass of ice
Q804330.s: Peru’s Cordillera Blanca is well named: a white wall of glaciers and fluted ice peaks only about nine degrees south of the equator, with more tropical glaciers than any other range on Earth. Its highest summit, Huascarán, reaches 6,768 m. Below, look for turquoise glacial lakes in the valleys and the green trench of the Santa River along its western foot.
Q804330.w: A line of brilliant white, fluted ice peaks with turquoise lakes in the valleys, running parallel to the Pacific coast.
f: Huascarán, 6,768 m, is the highest mountain in Peru.
Huascarán National Park, which covers the range, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The giant Puya raimondii, a relative of the pineapple, grows on its slopes; its flower spike can reach about 10 m.

q.q: Which is the highest mountain in Peru?

Q4794486.t: The Andes’ eastern arm, reaching into Venezuela
Q4794486.s: The easternmost of Colombia’s three Andean ranges carries Bogotá on its high plateau, then splits near the Venezuelan border. One arm, the Sierra de Perijá, heads north; the other, the Mérida Andes, runs north-east through Venezuela. Between them lies the vast blue sheet of Lake Maracaibo, so from above the mountains seem to hold it in a pincer.
Q4794486.w: Rugged green-and-brown ridges; to the north-west, the wide blue expanse of Lake Maracaibo held between two mountain arms.
f: Bogotá sits on a high plateau of this range at about 2,600 m.
Pico Bolívar, 4,978 m, in the Mérida Andes, is the highest peak in Venezuela.
Over the south-western shore of Lake Maracaibo, storms flash on more than a hundred nights a year — the Catatumbo lightning.

q.q: Which lake lies between the two arms of this cordillera?

Q233770.t: Australia’s wild northern wedge, pointing at New Guinea
Q233770.s: Cape York is one of the last great wild places in Australia: a long triangle of savanna, woodland and rainforest reaching north towards New Guinea, with few sealed roads. From above, look for red earth, braided rivers that flood in the wet season, and, off the east coast, the turquoise shallows of the Great Barrier Reef lying close to shore.
Q233770.w: Red earth and grey-green woodland cut by braided rivers, with the Great Barrier Reef’s turquoise shallows just off the east coast.
f: The tip of Cape York is the northernmost point of mainland Australia.
The Torres Strait, about 150 km wide, separates the peninsula from New Guinea.
Towering termite mounds, some several metres tall, dot the savanna.

q.q: Which island lies across the Torres Strait from Cape York?

Q7835.t: A diamond of steppe with a mountain rim on the Black Sea
Q7835.s: Crimea hangs from the mainland by a narrow neck, the Isthmus of Perekop, and from above its shape is unmistakable. Most of it is flat, dry steppe patterned with fields and shallow salt lakes; along the south coast the Crimean Mountains rise in a rim of limestone cliffs above the sea. To the north-east lie the shallow, sometimes pink-tinted lagoons of the Sivash.
Q7835.w: A diamond-shaped peninsula of flat steppe and salt lakes, with a mountain rim along the south coast and shallow lagoons to the north-east.
f: The Isthmus of Perekop, which joins Crimea to the mainland, is only about 7 km wide at its narrowest.
Roman-Kosh, 1,545 m, is the highest peak of the Crimean Mountains.
The Sivash lagoons are so salty that in places their water turns pink with algae.

q.q: What is the narrow neck joining Crimea to the mainland called?

Q165608.t: Ancient rock, tundra and lakes beyond the Arctic Circle
Q165608.s: Almost the whole Kola Peninsula lies north of the Arctic Circle, yet thanks to the warm North Atlantic Current its northern coast stays ice-free all year. From the window it is a rolling mosaic of tundra, dark forest and countless lakes on some of the oldest rock in Europe, with the bare Khibiny Mountains rising in the middle. On winter nights, look for the northern lights.
Q165608.w: Low, rolling tundra and dark forest dotted with countless lakes, and the bare, flat-topped Khibiny massif near the centre.
f: Murmansk, on the Kola coast, is the largest city north of the Arctic Circle.
The Kola Superdeep Borehole reached about 12.2 km — the deepest hole ever drilled.
The Khibiny Mountains are rich in apatite, which is mined to make fertiliser.

q.q: What record does the Kola Superdeep Borehole hold?

Q1394226.t: Vietnam’s southern tip, still growing into the sea
Q1394226.s: Mainland Vietnam ends here in a low, green wedge of mangroves and mudflats, with the sea on three sides. From cruise height it is a watery maze: winding channels, neat rectangles of shrimp ponds and dense dark-green forest. The land is still growing, as silt carried by the Mekong settles among the mangrove roots and pushes the shore outwards.
Q1394226.w: A low green tip of land laced with channels, dark mangrove forest and rectangular shrimp ponds, surrounded by muddy brown sea.
f: Cape Cà Mau is the southernmost point of mainland Vietnam.
Its mangroves are protected in Mũi Cà Mau National Park, a Ramsar wetland of international importance.

q.q: What is slowly pushing Cà Mau’s shore out to sea?

Q178543.t: A 1,200-km desert finger between ocean and gulf
Q178543.s: Baja California runs about 1,200 km south from the US border, a slender desert finger between the Pacific and the Gulf of California. From 11 km up the contrast is striking: rugged, bare mountains down its spine, cactus-dotted plains, and on the gulf side water of an almost unreal blue. Grey whales come each winter to calve in its Pacific lagoons.
Q178543.w: A long, narrow desert peninsula: bare brown mountains, pale lagoons on the Pacific side and deep-blue gulf waters to the east.
f: Its Pacific lagoons, such as Ojo de Liebre and San Ignacio, are among the grey whale’s main breeding grounds.
The Gulf of California is often called “the world’s aquarium”, a phrase attributed to Jacques Cousteau.
The gulf is slowly widening as the peninsula moves north-west with the Pacific plate.

q.q: Which whales come each winter to calve in Baja’s Pacific lagoons?

Q130978.t: A flat limestone slab with no rivers, only cenotes
Q130978.s: The Yucatán is as flat as a table: a vast slab of limestone covered in low green forest, with almost no rivers on the surface. Rain sinks straight through the rock into underground rivers, which surface in sinkholes called cenotes. At its northern tip lies the buried Chicxulub crater, left by the asteroid that ended the age of the dinosaurs 66 million years ago.
Q130978.w: Endless flat, low green forest with no hills or rivers; turquoise Caribbean coast to the east, cities like Mérida in the north.
f: A curved ring of cenotes in the north of the peninsula traces the buried rim of the Chicxulub crater.
Calakmul, one of the greatest Maya cities, lies hidden in the forest near the peninsula’s southern base.

q.q: What are the Yucatán’s water-filled sinkholes called?

Q60064.t: A volcanic arm reaching out towards the Aleutians
Q60064.s: The Alaska Peninsula stretches about 800 km south-west from the mainland, a rugged arm of volcanoes, lakes and tundra that leads into the Aleutian chain. From above, snowy cones rise one after another along its spine. In Katmai, in 1912, Novarupta produced the largest volcanic eruption of the 20th century, filling a valley with ash that steamed for years.
Q60064.w: A long, narrow arm of tundra and big lakes with a spine of snow-capped volcanoes, between the Pacific and Bristol Bay.
f: The 1912 eruption created the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes, named for its countless steaming vents.
Brooks Falls in Katmai National Park is famous for brown bears catching leaping salmon.
Aniakchak, a caldera about 10 km across, is one of the least-visited national monuments in the US.

q.q: Which valley was created by the 1912 Novarupta eruption?
q.a: The Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes

Q812.t: A low limestone peninsula brimming with water
Q812.s: Florida is one of the flattest places in the United States — its highest point is just 105 m above sea level — and from above it seems as much water as land. Countless round lakes dot the centre, Lake Okeechobee shines like a coin in the south, and below it the Everglades spread as a vast, slow-moving river of grass. Long sandy barrier islands line both coasts.
Q812.w: Flat green land freckled with round lakes, the big disc of Lake Okeechobee, and thin white barrier islands along both coasts.
f: Britton Hill, Florida’s highest point at 105 m, is the lowest state high point in the US.
The Everglades are a shallow sheet of water creeping south through sawgrass, often called a “river of grass”.
Many of central Florida’s round lakes are sinkholes in the limestone beneath.

q.q: What are the Everglades often called?

Q213237.t: Patagonia’s axe-head peninsula, a nursery for whales
Q213237.s: On the map Península Valdés looks like an axe head attached to the coast of Patagonia by a thin handle, the Carlos Ameghino Isthmus. The gulfs on either side, San José and Nuevo, are sheltered nurseries where southern right whales gather to calve from about June to December. The land itself is flat, dry steppe, with white salt pans in the middle.
Q213237.w: A roughly square peninsula of pale brown steppe on a narrow neck, with sheltered gulfs on either side and white salt pans inside.
f: Península Valdés is a UNESCO World Heritage Site for its marine mammals.
At Punta Norte, orcas deliberately beach themselves to snatch sea lion pups from the shore.

q.q: Which whales gather to calve in the gulfs of Valdés?

Q858306.t: China’s rocky thumb between the Bohai and the Yellow Sea
Q858306.s: The Shandong Peninsula juts east like a thumb between the Bohai Sea and the Yellow Sea, pointing towards Korea. From the window it is a patchwork of orchards and fields on rolling hills, with granite mountains near the coast and busy port cities strung along it. Qingdao sits on its southern shore beside the almost enclosed Jiaozhou Bay, crossed by one of the world’s longest sea bridges.
Q858306.w: A hilly peninsula of fields and orchards between two seas, with the rounded Jiaozhou Bay and Qingdao on the southern coast.
f: Laoshan, a granite mountain near Qingdao, rises about 1,130 m straight from the sea and is famous for its Taoist temples.
Qingdao’s famous brewery was founded in 1903.
The Jiaozhou Bay Bridge runs for about 26 km over the water.

q.q: Which city lies on Jiaozhou Bay?

Q131377.t: Red dunes meeting a cold, foggy ocean
Q131377.s: The Namib may be the oldest desert on Earth, dry for tens of millions of years. In its central sand sea, around Sossusvlei, the dunes rise over 300 m and glow brick-red in low sun, lined up in rows that run almost to the Atlantic. The cold ocean current brings fog instead of rain, and beetles, lizards and plants survive by drinking it.
Q131377.w: Endless rows of red-orange dunes running towards the coast, pale clay pans between them, and a white line of surf and fog.
f: The Namib Sand Sea is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
In Deadvlei, a white clay pan among the dunes, stand camel thorn trees that died centuries ago.
Fog-basking beetles tilt their backs into the wind so that droplets roll down into their mouths.

q.q: Where does the Namib get most of its moisture?

Q14314106.t: Egypt’s great desert of oases and white chalk towers
Q14314106.s: West of the Nile, Egypt is almost all desert: flat sand and stone plains broken by deep depressions, where oases such as Siwa, Bahariya, Farafra, Dakhla and Kharga drink from ancient groundwater. From cruise height, look for green specks of fields and palm groves in these basins. Near Farafra lies the White Desert, where the wind has carved chalk into mushroom-shaped towers.
Q14314106.w: Endless beige plains and escarpments, deep basins with green specks of oasis farms, and in places dazzling white chalk ground.
f: The Qattara Depression in the north drops to about 133 m below sea level, one of the lowest points in Africa.
The oases draw on the Nubian Sandstone Aquifer, one of the largest stores of fossil groundwater on Earth.

q.q: What carved the White Desert’s mushroom-shaped rocks?

Q464909.t: The Nile’s great bend through a stony desert
Q464909.s: East of the Nile in northern Sudan lies the Nubian Desert, an almost rainless plain of sandstone and granite crossed by dry wadis. From 11 km up, the most striking sight is the Nile itself: a thin green ribbon looping through the desert in a huge S-shaped bend. Along its banks stand the pyramids of Meroë and of Nubia’s other ancient kingdoms.
Q464909.w: A flat, pale stony plain with dark hills and dry wadis; to the west, the Nile’s green ribbon winding through a great bend.
f: Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt, many of them at Meroë.
The railway from Wadi Halfa to Abu Hamad, built in the late 1890s, runs almost straight across the desert.

q.q: Which ancient Nubian city is famous for its steep pyramids?

Q326896.t: Endless parallel red dunes in Australia’s north-west
Q326896.s: From the air the Great Sandy Desert looks combed: long, straight red dunes run side by side for hundreds of kilometres, separated by corridors of pale spinifex grass. It is one of the emptiest parts of Australia, home mainly to Aboriginal communities. Near its northern edge lies Wolfe Creek Crater, a near-perfect ring about 900 m across.
Q326896.w: Long, straight, parallel red dune ridges with pale grey-green spinifex between them, and the occasional white salt lake.
f: Wolfe Creek Crater is one of the best-preserved meteorite craters on Earth.
Australia’s dunes line up with the prevailing winds, forming a giant swirl around the centre of the continent.

q.q: What made Wolfe Creek Crater?

Q145165.t: Australia’s largest desert, red sand under blue-green scrub
Q145165.s: Australia’s largest desert covers some 350,000 km² — more than Italy. Yet it is far from bare: from above, its red dunes and sandhills are speckled with grey-green spinifex, mulga and mallee eucalypts. Dazzling white salt lakes mark its edges, and to the south the land flattens into the treeless Nullarbor Plain.
Q145165.w: Red sand ridges speckled with grey-green scrub, scattered white salt lakes, and flat, treeless plain to the south.
f: The explorer Ernest Giles named it in 1875 after Queen Victoria.
The Anangu Pitjantjatjara people have lived in and around this desert for many thousands of years.

q.q: Which is Australia’s largest desert?

Q172691.t: India’s Great Desert, surprisingly full of people
Q172691.s: The Thar, or Great Indian Desert, spreads across Rajasthan and into Pakistan, a land of wind-rippled dunes, thorn scrub and scattered villages. It is one of the most densely populated deserts in the world. Look for the long green line of the Indira Gandhi Canal cutting through the sand, bringing Himalayan river water to new fields.
Q172691.w: Tawny dunes and scrub dotted with villages, and a straight green corridor of canal and fields cutting across the sand.
f: Jaisalmer, the “Golden City”, is built of yellow sandstone and rises from the desert around a hilltop fort.
The Indira Gandhi Canal, one of the longest in India, carries water from the Sutlej and Beas rivers into the desert.

q.q: Which city in the Thar is known as the Golden City?

Q339162.t: A vast stony plain between the Levant and the Euphrates
Q339162.s: Between the green coast of the Levant and the Euphrates valley stretches the Syrian Desert, a vast plain of gravel and basalt rather than sand. From above it is flat and beige, crossed by straight roads, with dark lava fields in the south-west. For millennia caravans crossed it between the Mediterranean and Mesopotamia, stopping at the oasis of Palmyra.
Q339162.w: A flat, featureless beige plain with straight roads and dry wadis, and dark patches of basalt lava fields in the south-west.
f: The Harrat al-Sham basalt field in the south-west is one of the largest volcanic fields in the Middle East.
Ancient “desert kites” — huge stone-walled traps for hunting gazelles — were first noticed by pilots in the 1920s.

q.q: Which ancient caravan city grew in an oasis of the Syrian Desert?

Q172702.t: The Black Sands, and a crater burning for decades
Q172702.s: Karakum means “black sands”, though from above the dunes look tawny-grey, pinned down by saxaul and grass. The desert covers most of Turkmenistan. Near Derweze a gas crater about 70 m wide has been burning for decades, and at night its orange glow is a startling sight. Along the south runs the long green thread of the Karakum Canal.
Q172702.w: Grey-tawny dunes pinned by scrub, the green Karakum Canal to the south, and at night a small orange glow near Derweze.
f: The Karakum Canal, over 1,000 km long, carries Amu Darya water across the desert — one of the world’s longest irrigation canals.
The Karakum covers about 70% of Turkmenistan.

q.q: What does the name Karakum mean?

Q184364.t: The Red Sands between Central Asia’s two great rivers
Q184364.s: Kyzylkum means “red sands”, and the desert fills the land between the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, the two rivers that once fed the Aral Sea. From the window it is a reddish-beige plain of dunes and scrub, broken by bare rocky hills and salt flats. Here too lies Muruntau, one of the largest open-pit gold mines on Earth — a giant grey hole plain to see from the air.
Q184364.w: Reddish-beige dunes and scrub, bare rocky hills and white salt flats, and in places the huge grey stepped pit of the Muruntau mine.
f: The Muruntau gold mine’s open pit is more than 3 km long and hundreds of metres deep.
Since the 1960s the Aral Sea to the north-west has shrunk dramatically, as river water was taken to irrigate fields.

q.q: What does the name Kyzylkum mean?

Q47141.t: The driest place outside the poles, under crystal skies
Q47141.s: Some weather stations in the Atacama have never recorded rain. From cruise height it is a moonscape of salt flats, bare brown ranges and pastel-coloured volcanoes, with the Andes on one side and the cold Pacific on the other. The air is so dry and clear that some of the world’s largest telescopes have been built on its peaks.
Q47141.w: Bare brown and ochre ranges, white salt flats such as the Salar de Atacama, and snow-capped volcanoes along the eastern skyline.
f: The Salar de Atacama is Chile’s largest salt flat and one of the world’s main sources of lithium.
NASA has tested Mars rovers in the Atacama because its soil is so much like that of Mars.
ALMA, a giant array of radio telescopes, stands on a plateau at about 5,000 m.

q.q: Which metal is extracted in large amounts from the Salar de Atacama?

Q392250.t: Mexico’s narrow waist, where winds rush between oceans
Q392250.s: Here Mexico narrows to its waist: only about 200 km of land separate the Atlantic from the Pacific. The mountains dip low into a wide gap, and in winter strong northerly winds, the Tehuanos, funnel through it and burst out over the Pacific, whipping up the sea for hundreds of kilometres offshore. Near the Pacific coast, wide, shallow lagoons shine silver.
Q392250.w: A narrow land bridge with low hills in the middle, green lowlands to the north and dry plains and lagoons along the Pacific.
f: The Tehuano winds can blow at more than 100 km/h and are felt far out over the Pacific.
A railway has linked the two coasts across the isthmus since 1907.
The isthmus is often taken as the geographical boundary between North and Central America.

q.q: About how wide is the Isthmus of Tehuantepec?

Q182139.t: The land bridge that joined two continents
Q182139.s: This slender, S-shaped strip of land joins two continents and parts two oceans. When it rose from the sea about 3 million years ago, animals crossed between the Americas and ocean currents changed course. In the west the Panama Canal cuts through it; in the east the rainforest of the Darién is so wild that the Pan-American Highway stops at its edge.
Q182139.w: A narrow, winding strip of green between two seas: unbroken rainforest in the east, the canal and Gatún Lake in the west.
f: The Panama Canal, opened in 1914, is about 80 km long.
The Darién Gap is the only break in the Pan-American Highway between Alaska and the far south of South America.
Because the isthmus curves, the canal runs from the Atlantic in the north-west to the Pacific in the south-east.

q.q: In which year did the Panama Canal open?

Q322356.t: The Malay Peninsula’s narrowest neck, between two seas
Q322356.s: At the Kra Isthmus the Malay Peninsula pinches to its narrowest, about 44 km wide, with the Andaman Sea to the west and the Gulf of Thailand to the east. From 11 km up you may see both coasts at once: mangrove-fringed estuaries on one side, long sandy beaches on the other, and rubber and oil palm plantations in between. For centuries people have dreamed of cutting a canal here.
Q322356.w: A narrow neck of green hills and plantations with the sea visible on both sides, and the Kra River estuary to the west.
f: A canal across the Kra has been proposed since at least the 17th century, but it has never been built.
At the narrowest point the Kraburi River forms part of the border between Thailand and Myanmar.

q.q: Roughly how wide is the Kra Isthmus at its narrowest?

Q426977.t: Red-clay hills between the Appalachians and the coast
Q426977.s: Between the Blue Ridge and the flat coastal plain lies the Piedmont — literally the “foot of the mountains” — a rolling upland of red clay, pine woods and farms. From above, look for big reservoirs with branching, finger-like arms, such as Lake Hartwell and Lake Thurmond on the Savannah River. At its seaward edge rivers tumble over the Fall Line, where cities like Richmond, Columbia and Augusta grew up.
Q426977.w: Rolling green hills and woods with reddish fields, and large reservoirs with long, branching arms along the rivers.
f: The Fall Line cities grew where river boats could go no further upstream.
The Piedmont’s red colour comes from iron-rich clay soils.
Atlanta and Charlotte, two of the largest cities in the American South, stand on the Piedmont.

q.q: What does the name Piedmont mean?

Q743261.t: Cloud forest tumbling from the Andes to the Amazon
Q743261.s: On the eastern flank of the Bolivian Andes the land drops from icy ridges to steamy lowlands within a few dozen kilometres, and the Yungas fill that slope with cloud forest. From the window, look for a wall of dark green veiled in cloud, cut by deep, winding valleys where rivers rush down towards the Amazon basin. Coffee, coca and citrus grow on its terraces.
Q743261.w: Steep, dark-green slopes veiled in cloud, dropping from the snowy Andes to the flat Amazon lowlands and cut by deep valleys.
f: The Yungas descend more than 3,000 m, from the high Andes to the Amazon lowlands.
Their cloud forests are among the richest on Earth in species, especially orchids and birds.

q.q: Where do the Yungas lie?
q.a: On the eastern slopes of the Andes

Q206650.t: New Zealand’s glacier-draped spine along a great fault
Q206650.s: The Southern Alps run the length of New Zealand’s South Island, rising abruptly along the Alpine Fault, where two tectonic plates meet. Westerly winds dump huge amounts of rain and snow on them, so glaciers reach down almost into the rainforest of the west coast, while the east lies in a dry rain shadow. On the eastern side, look for lakes of an unreal milky turquoise, such as Pukaki and Tekapo.
Q206650.w: A snowy, glacier-streaked spine with rainforest to the west, and tawny plains and turquoise lakes to the east.
f: Aoraki / Mount Cook, 3,724 m, is New Zealand’s highest peak.
The Franz Josef and Fox glaciers descend to within a few hundred metres of sea level, into temperate rainforest.
The Tasman Glacier, about 23 km long, is the longest in New Zealand.

q.q: Which is New Zealand’s highest peak?

ne-rg-1730071499.t: Remote sandstone hills above Central Africa’s savannas
ne-rg-1730071499.s: In the far north-east of the Central African Republic, a rugged sandstone massif rises above the savanna — the Bongo Massif, also called the Chaîne des Mongos. It is one of the remotest places in Africa, with no towns and hardly any roads. From cruise height, look for dark, wooded escarpments over a pale-green sea of grass, threaded with darker lines of forest along the rivers.
ne-rg-1730071499.w: Dark, wooded sandstone escarpments rising from pale savanna, with thin dark lines of gallery forest along the rivers.
f: North of the massif lies Manovo-Gounda St Floris, the largest national park in Central Africa’s savannas and a UNESCO site.
More than 300 bird species have been recorded on the park’s northern floodplains.

q.q: Which UNESCO national park stretches north of the Bongo Massif?

Q2961771.t: Hidden valleys where a million people lived unseen
Q2961771.s: A great mountain spine runs the length of New Guinea, and hidden among its ridges lie wide, fertile valleys. When outsiders first flew over them and trekked in during the 1930s, they found around a million people farming there, unknown to the wider world. From 11 km up, look for patchworks of gardens on the valley floors, framed by ridges of cloud forest.
Q2961771.w: Steep, cloud-wrapped forested ridges with broad green valleys below, their floors patterned with small garden plots.
f: Kuk Swamp in these highlands is one of the world’s earliest centres of farming and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Mount Wilhelm, 4,509 m, is the highest peak in Papua New Guinea.
Puncak Jaya, 4,884 m, in the range’s western part, is the highest island peak on Earth and still holds small equatorial glaciers.

q.q: When did outsiders first reach the populated highland valleys?

Q189915.t: Limestone mountains that gave the world the word “karst”
Q189915.s: Running parallel to the Adriatic from Slovenia to Albania, the Dinaric Alps are built of pale grey limestone, and from above they look bleached and pitted. Rain vanishes into the rock, leaving few surface rivers but countless sinkholes, caves and flat-floored basins called poljes. The word “karst”, used by geologists worldwide, comes from the Kras plateau at their northern end.
Q189915.w: Pale grey, pitted limestone ridges with green flat-floored basins, deep canyons, and the island-fringed Adriatic coast to the south-west.
f: The Tara River Canyon in Montenegro is about 1,300 m deep, one of the deepest in Europe.
The Plitvice Lakes, a chain of turquoise lakes linked by waterfalls, formed behind travertine dams in these mountains.

q.q: Which geological term comes from a plateau in the Dinaric Alps?

ne-rg-1730072787.t: A sandstone rampart south of the Hoggar mountains
ne-rg-1730072787.s: South of the dark volcanic Ahaggar lies a very different landscape: the Tassili Oua-n-Ahaggar, a broad sandstone plateau that the wind has carved into towers, arches and narrow corridors. From above it looks like a crumbling brown fortress wall, half drowned in drifting orange sand. It runs from southern Algeria towards the border with Niger, through one of the emptiest stretches of the Sahara.
ne-rg-1730072787.w: A broad brown plateau broken into blocks and towers by sand-filled corridors, with orange dunes lapping at its edges.
f: In the Tuareg language, “tassili” means “plateau”.
The plateau curves around the southern side of the Ahaggar massif.

q.q: What rock is this plateau mostly made of?

Q190048.t: A stone forest holding the Sahara’s greatest rock art
Q190048.s: Near the Libyan border, the Tassili n’Ajjer rises as a vast sandstone plateau eroded into a “forest” of pillars, arches and canyons. Its rock shelters hold more than 15,000 paintings and engravings — giraffes, hippos, herds of cattle, dancers — recording thousands of years of a greener Sahara. Look for a dark, ragged plateau edge with orange dunes piled at its foot.
Q190048.w: A dark, deeply eroded plateau cut into a maze of pillars and canyons, with orange dunes piled against its edges.
f: Tassili n’Ajjer has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1982.
Its name means “plateau of rivers” in the Tuareg language.
A few hundred ancient Saharan cypresses survive in its canyons; some are thought to be about 2,000 years old.

q.q: How many ancient paintings and engravings does Tassili n’Ajjer hold?

ne-rg-1730072795.t: A sea of sand dunes in the empty heart of Libya
ne-rg-1730072795.s: In eastern Libya, the Calanshio Sand Sea spreads long ridges of pale sand across a land with almost no rain and no permanent settlements. From the window, the dunes line up in parallel rows running roughly north to south, shaped by the prevailing wind, with flat gravel plains — sarirs — along their edges. Beneath this emptiness lie major oilfields and vast stores of ancient groundwater.
ne-rg-1730072795.w: Long parallel ridges of pale sand running north–south, flat grey gravel plains along the edges, and almost no sign of life.
f: Water pumped from beneath this desert flows north to Libya’s coast through the Great Man-Made River, a network of giant pipes.
The Sarir oilfield, one of Libya’s largest, lies on the edge of the sand sea.

q.q: What are the flat gravel plains around the Calanshio dunes called?

Q3056157.t: A remote dune sea, and a meteorite older than Earth
Q3056157.s: Erg Chech is one of the loneliest corners of the Sahara: a great sea of dunes on the border of Algeria and Mali, far from any road or oasis. From cruise height, look for long, orderly dune ridges broken by darker gravel plains and rocky outcrops. In 2020 a meteorite found here, Erg Chech 002, turned out to be one of the oldest volcanic rocks ever studied — about 4.56 billion years old.
Q3056157.w: Long, orderly orange dune ridges alternating with darker gravel plains and rocky outcrops, with no roads or oases in sight.
f: Erg Chech 002 is a piece of volcanic crust from an early protoplanet that formed before Earth itself.
Hot deserts are among the best places to find meteorites: dark stones stand out on pale ground and weather slowly.

q.q: What was found in Erg Chech in 2020?
x: A cave full of rock art

Q84127.t: Treeless tundra with a perfectly round crater lake
Q84127.s: At the northern tip of Quebec, the Ungava Peninsula is a vast, treeless tundra scraped bare by ice sheets, scattered with thousands of lakes and cut by rivers flowing to Hudson Bay and Ungava Bay. Near its northern end lies one of Canada’s most striking sights: Pingualuit Crater, a perfectly round lake about 3.4 km wide, punched out by a meteorite 1.4 million years ago.
Q84127.w: Bare, rolling tundra with countless lakes and rocky ridges; in the north, a single perfectly circular crater lake.
f: The lake in Pingualuit Crater holds some of the clearest fresh water in the world.
Nunavik, the Inuit homeland that covers the peninsula, has no road link to southern Quebec.

q.q: About how old is Pingualuit Crater?

Q1898305.t: The last ridges before the Sahara begins
Q1898305.s: Across Algeria runs the Saharan Atlas, a series of parallel ridges — the Ksour, Djebel Amour and Ouled Naïl mountains — that marks the northern edge of the Sahara. North of them lie the High Plateaus with their shallow salt lakes, the chotts; south of them the desert begins. From 11 km up, look for folded, rust-coloured ridges running south-west to north-east, with stony plains stretching beyond.
Q1898305.w: Parallel folded ridges running south-west to north-east, pale salt lakes to the north and open desert to the south.
f: Oasis towns such as Laghouat grew at the range’s southern foot, where water flows out of the mountains.
The Chott ech Chergui, north of the range, is one of the largest salt lakes in North Africa.

q.q: What are the shallow salt lakes north of the Saharan Atlas called?

ne-rg-1730073347.t: The western wall of Africa’s great rift lakes
ne-rg-1730073347.s: Along the eastern edge of the Congo, the Mitumba Mountains rise as the western shoulder of the Albertine Rift, a great crack in Africa’s crust. From above they are a long, forested wall dropping steeply to a string of rift lakes — Albert, Edward, Kivu and Tanganyika. Near their southern end, look for the long, dark-blue trough of Lake Tanganyika below the ridges.
ne-rg-1730073347.w: A long, steep forested escarpment with the deep blue of Lake Tanganyika or Lake Kivu in the rift valley below.
f: Lake Tanganyika, at the foot of the range, is the second-deepest lake in the world, about 1,470 m.
Lake Tanganyika is also the longest freshwater lake on Earth, about 670 km.

q.q: Which deep rift lake lies below the southern Mitumba Mountains?

ne-rg-1730073365.t: Red-earth plateaus that fill the world’s coffee cups
ne-rg-1730073365.s: Behind Vietnam’s coast, the land climbs onto the Central Highlands, a series of basalt plateaus with rich red soil. From the window, look for a green-and-rust patchwork: rows of coffee bushes, pepper and rubber plantations, and scattered volcanic cones and lakes. Most of Vietnam’s coffee grows here, helping make the country the world’s second-largest coffee producer.
ne-rg-1730073365.w: Rolling red-earth plateaus patterned with green plantations, a few rounded volcanic cones, and forested mountains to the east.
f: Buôn Ma Thuột is often called Vietnam’s coffee capital.
Most of the coffee grown here is robusta, a hardier species with a stronger taste than arabica.

q.q: Which crop has made Vietnam’s Central Highlands famous?

ne-rg-1730073373.t: Siberia’s wild ridges between the Yenisei and Baikal
ne-rg-1730073373.s: The Eastern Sayan stretch about 1,000 km from the Yenisei towards Lake Baikal, a wilderness of sharp, bare peaks, deep valleys and taiga. From cruise height you see ridge after ridge streaked with snow for much of the year, and rivers such as the Kan and the Oka running out towards the Yenisei and the Angara. The highest peak, Munku-Sardyk, stands on the border with Mongolia.
ne-rg-1730073373.w: Ridge after ridge of sharp, snow-streaked peaks with dark taiga in the valleys, stretching south-east towards Baikal.
f: Munku-Sardyk, 3,491 m, is the highest peak of the Eastern Sayan.
The Tofalars, one of Russia’s smallest peoples, live in the remote northern valleys of the range.
In the Valley of Volcanoes on the Oka plateau, young lava fields and cones stand among the taiga.

q.q: Which is the highest peak of the Eastern Sayan?

Q201678.t: Where Siberia’s rivers part for two oceans
Q201678.s: The Yablonovy Range runs some 650 km across Transbaikalia, a line of rounded, forested ridges that hardly looks like a great barrier. Yet it is one: rain on its western slopes flows through the Selenga and Baikal towards the Arctic Ocean, while rain on the east ends up in the Amur and the Pacific. The city of Chita lies at its eastern foot.
Q201678.w: Low, rounded, dark-forested ridges running north-east, wide valleys, and the city of Chita at the south-eastern foot.
f: The Trans-Siberian Railway crosses the range at the Yablonovy Pass, just west of Chita.
The name sounds like the Russian word for “apple”, but its real origin is disputed.

q.q: Which city lies at the eastern foot of the Yablonovy Range?

ne-rg-1730073417.t: Dark mountains and lava fields along the Red Sea
ne-rg-1730073417.s: Along Arabia’s Red Sea coast, the Hejaz Mountains rise steeply from a narrow coastal plain and slope gently east into the interior. From 11 km up they are a jumble of dark granite and brown sandstone, with great black lava fields — harrats — spread across the plateau behind them. Near Al-Ula, look for warm-coloured sandstone cliffs and valleys where the Nabataeans carved their tombs.
ne-rg-1730073417.w: Steep dark mountains above a thin coastal strip, black lava fields on the plateau behind, and orange sandstone around Al-Ula.
f: Hegra, near Al-Ula, has more than 100 Nabataean tombs cut into sandstone and was Saudi Arabia’s first UNESCO site.
The Hejaz Railway, opened in 1908, ran through these mountains from Damascus to Medina.

q.q: What are Arabia’s black lava fields called?

Q730673.t: Arabia’s green, misty highlands above the Red Sea
Q730673.s: Surprisingly for Arabia, the Asir is green. These mountains in the south-west of the peninsula rise to about 3,000 m and catch monsoon rain and mist from the Red Sea, so their slopes carry juniper forest and ancient farming terraces. From above, look for a dark, rugged escarpment dropping sharply to the hot coastal plain of the Tihamah, with desert stretching away on the other side.
Q730673.w: A dark, rugged escarpment with a green tinge and terraced slopes, dropping steeply west to a hot coastal plain.
f: Jabal Sawda, near Abha, is about 3,000 m high and usually counted as Saudi Arabia’s highest peak.
Al-Qatt Al-Asiri, the bright geometric wall painting done by Asiri women, is on UNESCO’s intangible heritage list.

q.q: What makes the Asir Mountains unusually green for Arabia?

Q484725.t: A wall between the green Caspian and Iran’s dry plateau
Q484725.s: The Alborz form a sharp wall between two worlds: on the north, slopes of dense green Hyrcanian forest drop to the Caspian Sea; on the south, bare brown ridges face the dry Iranian plateau and the sprawl of Tehran. Rising above them all is Damavand, a lone, near-perfect volcanic cone about 5,600 m high, often white with snow even in summer.
Q484725.w: A lone, snow-capped volcanic cone above a long ridge, green forest on the Caspian side and bare brown slopes towards Tehran.
f: Damavand is the highest peak in Iran and the highest volcano in Asia.
The Hyrcanian forests on the northern slopes, relics of woodland millions of years old, are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Tehran spreads along the southern foot of the Alborz, its northern districts climbing the slopes.

q.q: Which lone volcanic cone is the highest peak in Iran?

Q143014.t: Where the Andes step down towards the Amazon and Chaco
Q143014.s: The Eastern Cordillera is the Andes’ eastern flank, where the mountains begin their long descent to the lowlands. In Bolivia it is a maze of red, ochre and green ridges cut by deep valleys, with the white colonial city of Sucre set among them at about 2,800 m. Further east the ridges soften into forested foothills and then the flat plains of the Chaco and the Amazon.
Q143014.w: Folded red, ochre and green ridges with deep valleys, fading eastwards into forested foothills and flat lowland plains.
f: Near Sucre, a quarry wall called Cal Orck’o preserves thousands of dinosaur footprints, tilted almost upright.
Sucre, Bolivia’s constitutional capital, is known as the White City for its whitewashed colonial buildings.

q.q: Which Bolivian city in the Eastern Cordillera is called the White City?

ne-rg-1730073543.t: Aboriginal stone country at the top of Australia
ne-rg-1730073543.s: Arnhem Land, in the north-east of Australia’s Northern Territory, is one of the country’s largest Aboriginal-owned regions, and visitors need a permit to enter. From the window you see a rugged sandstone plateau — the “stone country” — cut by gorges, then wide floodplains and mangrove-lined rivers that turn into shining sheets of water in the wet season. Its rock art is among the oldest and richest on Earth.
ne-rg-1730073543.w: A rugged, gorge-cut sandstone plateau, wide green floodplains and winding, mangrove-lined rivers flowing north.
f: The Yolŋu bark petitions, sent to Australia’s parliament in 1963, were a milestone in the Aboriginal land rights movement.
Arnhem Land’s rock art includes “X-ray” paintings that show the bones and organs of animals.

q.q: What do Arnhem Land’s famous “X-ray” rock paintings show?
q.a: The bones and organs of animals
